newsitem.title: USA: Common electronic banking use decades away - Citicorp.
newsitem.headline: Common electronic banking use decades away - Citicorp.

text.p: It will take at least half a century for customer use of electronic money and banking to become commonplace, the chairman of Citicorp said Thursday.

It will be 50 to 70 years before the majority of people do their business electronically, Citicorp Chairman John Reed said, noting that everyone was not yet comfortable using computers or the Internet.

"Cash machines have been around for 20-25 years, and for some people it's 100 percent of their life, but a significant number of people have never used them," Reed told a conference on electronic money and banking.

Issues related to privacy and security must be resolved for electronic banking to take off. Citicorp currently considers the Internet off-limits as a place to offer banking products until the security issues are solved, he said.

"The Internet is fundamentally flawed in that regard right now," Reed said. "At this moment in time at least, we at Citicorp would feel very uncomfortable accommodating any transactions on the Internet," he said.
Customers are "scared to death" that people will try to access their account or charge to their account, Reed said.
Citicorp has an electronic banking product for the Internet called "Web CAT," which stands for Customer Activated Terminal, but the bank does not feel comfortable using it yet, Reed said.

"It's alive and well in the labs, and it looks good, and feels good, and smells good," he said. "But we today would not feel comfortable consummating a transaction" such as allowing a customer to debit an account or pay a bill because of security concerns, Reed said.
Once electronic banking is in full swing, the structure of the marketplace is likely to change with more consolidation and some banks leaving the consumer side of the business, he said.
For the industry in the future "the ability to deal with consumers through software is going to be a required skill," Reed said.
Regulators said they were looking at how to oversee electronic commerce, and some said they wanted to be sure not to overregulate and hinder innovation.

"I suspect it makes sense to err on the side of under rather than overregulation with respect to these new payment systems," Robert Pitofsky, chairman of the Federal Trade Commission, said at the same conference.
